title: You Cannot Regulate a Child Into Thinking
author: Vicky Brooks
summary: Vicky Brooks, writing at Give Spark, argues that classroom regulation strategies such as movement breaks, calm corners and breathing routines can quietly turn from care into compliance. She says the vocabulary has changed from 'sit down and be quiet' to 'use your strategy', but if the aim is still a silent child returning to a passive task, nothing has changed. Her central complaint is that the intervention targets the child while the lesson stays the same, so children are regulated back into the very conditions that overwhelmed them. She suggests treating restlessness as information: when many children disengage at the same points, the pattern points to the task, and fill-in-the-blank or copying work demands little thinking. She is careful to say breaks are valuable, that not all dysregulation is caused by lessons, and that children must also learn to persist at unexciting work. Drawing on Stein and colleagues' research on how cognitive demand drains out of tasks, she concludes that regulation can make learning possible but cannot make a hollow task worth doing, and that engagement requires task design.
points: Brooks distinguishes regulation as care (helping a child feel safe and in control) from regulation as compliance (making a child calm enough to accept the same task), and the test is whether anyone investigates why the child struggled.
Treating each fidgeting or withdrawn child with an individual tool or strategy leaves the lesson design unquestioned, so the nervous system adapts repeatedly while the task never has to.
When restlessness appears across a class at the same points or in the same task types, teachers should read it as feedback about the task rather than only as a problem within the child.

Scheduled movement breaks are defended as anticipatory support, but Brooks warns they can substitute for examining what children return to, producing lessons children recover from rather than think through.
Cognitive engagement comes from design: tasks that ask students to predict, weigh, notice patterns, decide and defend give the mind somewhere to go, which no amount of calm can supply.
quotes: The words have changed. Instead of saying ‘Sit down, be quiet and do as you are told,’ we now say ‘Use your strategy, regulate your body and get ready to learn.’ But if the goal is still a quiet child returning to a passive task, nothing has really changed.

When we help a child feel safe, manage overwhelming emotions and regain a sense of control, regulation is an act of care. But if our only goal is to get them sitting quietly and working again, without investigating why they were struggling, we use regulation to make them easier to manage.
Then, once their body is calm enough, we return them to exactly the same experience. The same passive task. The same expectation to sit, listen, follow and finish.
A child can move while thinking deeply. They can also sit perfectly still while understanding very little. Stillness is not a reliable measure of either regulation or learning.
The child fidgets, so the child receives a tool. The child withdraws, so the child receives a strategy. The child cannot sustain attention, so the child receives a target.
If children repeatedly disengage during the same kinds of tasks, we should ask what their minds are being given to do. A reset every fifteen minutes does not remove the need to ask that question.
A calm body does not guarantee an active mind. A child can sit silently through an excellent explanation while thinking about lunch.
A task that asks a child to predict, weigh something, notice a pattern, decide and defend gives the mind somewhere to go.
